{{Short description|Infinite sequence in mathematics}}
[[File:Kolakoski_sequence_spiral.svg|thumb|300px|Visualisation of the 3rd to 50th terms of the Kolakoski sequence as a spiral. The terms start at the dot at the middle of the spiral. In the following revolution, each arc is repeated if the term is 1, or divided into two equal halves if it is 2. The first two terms cannot be shown as they are self-referential. In [http://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/1d/Kolakoski_sequence_spiral.svg the SVG image], hover over an arc or label to highlight it and show its statistics.]]

In [[mathematics]], the '''Kolakoski sequence''', sometimes also known as the '''Oldenburger–Kolakoski sequence''',<ref name=fractal /> is an [[infinite sequence]] of symbols {1,2} that is the sequence of run lengths in its own [[run-length encoding]].<ref name=PF93 /> It is named after the [[recreational mathematics|recreational mathematician]] [[William Kolakoski]] (1944–97) who described it in 1965,<ref name=AMM_Journal /> but it was previously discussed by [[Rufus Oldenburger]] in 1939.<ref name="fractal" /><ref name=Oldenburger />

==Definition==
[[File:Kolakoski run length.svg|thumb|256px|the Kolakoski sequence describes its own run length]]

The initial terms of the Kolakoski sequence are:

:1,2,2,1,1,2,1,2,2,1,2,2,1,1,2,1,1,2,2,1,2,1,1,2,1,2,2,1,1,... {{OEIS|A000002}}

Each symbol occurs in a "run" (a sequence of equal elements) of either one or two consecutive terms, and writing down the lengths of these runs gives exactly the same sequence:

:1,<u>2,2</u>,<u>1,1</u>,2,1,<u>2,2</u>,1,<u>2,2</u>,<u>1,1</u>,2,<u>1,1</u>,<u>2,2</u>,1,2,<u>1,1</u>,2,1,<u>2,2</u>,<u>1,1</u>,2,<u>1,1</u>,2,1,<u>2,2</u>,1,<u>2,2</u>,<u>1,1</u>,2,1,<u>2,2</u>,...

:1,&nbsp;2&nbsp;,&nbsp;2&nbsp;,1,1,&nbsp;2&nbsp;,1,&nbsp;2&nbsp;,&nbsp;2&nbsp;,1,&nbsp;2&nbsp;,&nbsp;2&nbsp;,1,1,&nbsp;2&nbsp;,1,1,&nbsp;2&nbsp;,&nbsp;2&nbsp;,1,&nbsp;2&nbsp;,1,1,&nbsp;2&nbsp;,1,&nbsp;2&nbsp;,&nbsp;2&nbsp;,1,1,&nbsp;2&nbsp;,...

The description of the Kolakoski sequence is therefore reversible. If ''K'' stands for "the Kolakoski sequence", description #1 logically implies description #2 (and vice versa):

:1. The terms of ''K'' are generated by the runs (i.e., run-lengths) of ''K''
:2. The runs of ''K'' are generated by the terms of ''K''

Accordingly, one can say that each term of the Kolakoski sequence generates a run of one or two future terms. The first 1 of the sequence generates a run of "1", i.e. itself; the first 2 generates a run of "22", which includes itself; the second 2 generates a run of "11"; and so on. Each number in the sequence is the ''length'' of the next run to be generated, and the ''element'' to be generated alternates between 1 and 2:

:1,2 (length of sequence ''l'' = 2; sum of terms ''s'' = 3)
:1,2,2 (''l'' = 3, ''s'' = 5)
:1,2,2,1,1 (''l'' = 5, ''s'' = 7)
:1,2,2,1,1,2,1 (''l'' = 7, ''s'' = 10)
:1,2,2,1,1,2,1,2,2,1 (''l'' = 10, ''s'' = 15)
:1,2,2,1,1,2,1,2,2,1,2,2,1,1,2 (''l'' = 15, ''s'' = 23)

As can be seen, the length of the sequence at each stage is equal to the sum of terms in the previous stage. This animation illustrates the process:

[[File:Kolakoski animated.gif|800px|center|An animated gif illustrating how later terms of the Kolakoski sequence are generated by earlier terms.]]

These self-generating properties, which remain if the sequence is written without the initial 1, mean that the Kolakoski sequence can be described as a [[fractal]], or mathematical object that encodes its own representation on other scales.<ref name=fractal /> Bertran Steinsky has created a recursive formula for the ''i''-th term of the sequence.<ref name=steinsky />

==Research==
=== Recurrence properties ===
The sequence is not eventually [[periodic function|periodic]], that is, its terms do not have a general repeating pattern (cf. [[irrational number]]s like [[Pi|π]] and [[Square root of 2|{{radic|2}}]]). More generally, the sequence is cube-free, i.e., has no substring of the form <math>www</math> with <math>w</math> some nonempty finite string.<ref name="Carpi">{{cite journal|last=Carpi|first=Arturo|title=On repeated factors in <math>C^\infty</math>-words|language=en|journal=Information Processing Letters|volume=52|issue=6|pages=289–294|date=1994|issn=0020-0190|doi=10.1016/0020-0190(94)00162-6|mr=1307746|zbl=0938.68698}}</ref> It is not known whether every string appearing in the sequence occurs infinitely many times, nor whether the occurrence of a string implies the occurrence of its reverse string; the two facts, however, are known to be equivalent.<ref name="Della Corte">{{cite journal|last=Della Corte|first=Alessandro|title=Kolakoski sequence: links between recurrence, symmetry and limit density |language=en|journal=Open Journal of Discrete Applied Mathematics|volume=4|issue=1|pages=29–44|date=2020|doi=10.30538/psrp-odam2021.0052|arxiv=2002.08306}}</ref>

===Density===

It seems plausible that the density of 1s in the Kolakoski {1,2}-sequence is 1/2, but this conjecture remains unproved.<ref name=clark_kimberling /> [[Václav Chvátal]] has proved that the upper density of 1s is less than 0.50084.<ref name=vaclav_chvatal /> Nilsson has used the same method with far greater computational power to obtain the bound 0.500080.<ref name=Nilsson />

Although calculations of the first 3×10<sup>8</sup> values of the sequence appeared to show its density converging to a value slightly different from 1/2,<ref name=steinsky /> later calculations that extended the sequence to its first 10<sup>13</sup> values show the deviation from a density of 1/2 growing smaller, as one would expect if the limiting density actually is 1/2.<ref name="n"/>

===Connection with tag systems===
The Kolakoski sequence can also be described as the result of a simple cyclic [[tag system]]. However, as this system is a 2-tag system rather than a 1-tag system (that is, it replaces pairs of symbols by other sequences of symbols, rather than operating on a single symbol at a time) it lies in the region of parameters for which tag systems are [[Turing complete]], making it difficult to use this representation to reason about the sequence.{{r|vdp}}

==Algorithms==
The Kolakoski sequence may be generated by an [[algorithm]] that, in the ''i''-th iteration, reads the value ''x''<sub>''i''</sub> that has already been output as the ''i''-th value of the sequence (or, if no such value has been output yet, sets ''x''<sub>''i''</sub>&nbsp;=&nbsp;''i''). Then, if ''i'' is odd, it outputs ''x''<sub>''i''</sub> copies of the number 1, while if ''i'' is even, it outputs ''x''<sub>''i''</sub> copies of the number 2.
Thus, the first few steps of the algorithm are:
#The first value has not yet been output, so set ''x''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;=&nbsp;1, and output 1 copy of the number 1
#The second value has not yet been output, so set ''x''<sub>2</sub>&nbsp;=&nbsp;2, and output 2 copies of the number 2
#The third value ''x''<sub>3</sub> was output as 2 in the second step, so output 2 copies of the number 1.
#The fourth value ''x''<sub>4</sub> was output as 1 in the third step, so output 1 copy of the number 2. Etc.

This algorithm takes [[linear time]], but because it needs to refer back to earlier positions in the sequence it needs to store the whole sequence, taking linear space. An alternative algorithm that generates multiple copies of the sequence at different speeds, with each copy of the sequence using the output of the previous copy to determine what to do at each step, can be used to generate the sequence in linear time and only [[L (complexity)|logarithmic space]].<ref name="n" />
